content: Smooth muscle tumors (SMTs), which include leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, have recently been identified in many children infected with HIV. Leiomyosarcoma has emerged as the second most common malignancy in children with HIV or other immunodeficiency disorders in the United States. Although leiomyosarcoma represents only 2% to 4% of childhood soft tissue sarcomas, its prognosis is significantly worse in HIV-infected patients compared to those who are not infected. The development of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated SMTs in children with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) leads to a decline in overall health, a reduction in quality of life, and frequently results in death. Some researchers attribute the primary cause of death in these cases to SMTs rather than AIDS itself. Currently, there is no consensus on the optimal therapeutic approach for these tumors, and there is a pressing need to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various treatments for AIDS-associated SMTs in terms of overall survival and disease-free survival in children. To address this, a systematic review was conducted to assess the effectiveness of current therapeutic interventions for children with AIDS-associated leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma who had not received prior treatment. A comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane HIV/AIDS Group trials register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, was performed. The search spanned from 1966 to 2009 and included both published and unpublished studies, as well as conference proceedings and reference lists. No language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or controlled clinical trials (CCTs) evaluating therapies for leiomyosarcoma and leiomyoma in children with AIDS. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, retrieved full texts of potentially relevant studies, and assessed their quality using predefined criteria. However, no eligible RCTs or CCTs were identified. The absence of RCTs or CCTs means that current clinical practice for treating SMTs in HIV-infected children relies on descriptive studies and situational analyses. As a result, there is insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy and acceptability of existing interventions. Clinicians are advised to approach treatment on a case-by-case basis until robust evidence becomes available. Future research must prioritize the design and execution of high-quality RCTs to provide definitive conclusions. Multicenter, randomized, double-blind controlled trials are urgently needed to evaluate the effectiveness of therapies for AIDS-associated SMTs, with the goal of improving survival rates and reducing mortality in this population. Policymakers and researchers should allocate funding to support these trials, thereby increasing the quantity and quality of evidence in this area. Additionally, safety and adverse events should be rigorously monitored using standardized systems, and long-term adverse effects in children with HIV should be carefully evaluated.
